learn.title: How Wind Turbines Generate Power 🌬️
learn.intro: Wind turbines convert wind's kinetic energy into electricity, offering a clean alternative to fossil fuels. They play a critical role in reducing carbon emissions and advancing the global energy transition by providing sustainable power without greenhouse gases.
learn.c1_text: Wind turbines use blade designs optimized for aerodynamics to capture wind energy. As wind flows over the blades, it creates lift, spinning the rotor. This mechanical energy is then transferred to a generator. A 2 MW turbine can produce ~5.5 million kWh annually, enough to power 500 homes.
learn.c2_text: The spinning rotor drives a generator, which uses electromagnetic induction to produce electricity. Modern turbines often use permanent magnet generators for higher efficiency. For example, a 1.5 MW turbine might achieve 40% efficiency, generating consistent power even in moderate winds.
learn.c3_text: Electricity from turbines is fed into the grid via transformers. In India, small wind turbines are being deployed in rural areas, with projects like Tamil Nadu's 5 MW community wind farms providing 24/7 power to 1,000+ households.
learn.stat1: Global wind capacity reached 900 GW in 2023, supplying 7% of world electricity.
learn.stat2: A single offshore turbine can generate 12-18 MW, equivalent to powering 10,000 homes.
learn.stat3: India's wind energy potential is 402 GW, with 46 GW installed as of 2024.
learn.stat4: Small turbines (up to 100 kW) can meet 30-50% of a home's energy needs in windy regions.

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage: The World's Largest Battery 💧
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage acts as a giant battery by moving water between reservoirs. It stores excess electricity during low demand and releases it during peaks, crucial for balancing grids reliant on intermittent renewables like solar and wind.
learn.c1_text: Excess electricity pumps water from a lower to a higher reservoir. When needed, water flows back down through turbines, generating power. A 1 GW plant can store 2-3 GWh, enough to power 200,000 homes for 4 hours.
learn.c2_text: These systems achieve 70-85% efficiency, making them cost-effective for large-scale storage. The Bath County Pumped Storage Station in the US holds 30.3 TWh annually, demonstrating their massive capacity.
learn.c3_text: India has 15,000 MW potential in pumped hydro, with projects like the Hemavati Reservoir in Karnataka aiming to store 2 GW. This supports India's 500 GW renewable target by 2030.
learn.stat1: Global pumped hydro accounts for 95% of grid storage capacity, with 160 GW installed worldwide.
learn.stat2: A single plant can reduce grid emissions by 20-30 million tons annually.
learn.stat3: India's National Energy Policy aims to triple pumped hydro capacity by 2030.
learn.stat4: Pumped hydro can store energy for 24+ hours, ideal for seasonal renewable surplus.

learn.title: Offshore Wind Farms: Harnessing Sea Winds 🌊
learn.intro: Offshore wind farms leverage strong, consistent coastal winds to generate vast amounts of electricity. They are critical for scaling renewable energy, especially in densely populated coastal regions.
learn.c1_text: Turbines are mounted on floating platforms or fixed foundations in deep water. For example, the UK's Hornsea Project uses 200 turbines to generate 1.4 GW, enough to power 1 million homes. Site selection considers wind patterns and marine conditions.
learn.c2_text: Electricity is transmitted via undersea cables to onshore grids. Offshore farms often use HVDC (High-Voltage Direct Current) cables for efficiency. Germany's Borkum Riffgrund project uses 78 turbines connected via 100 km of cable.
learn.c3_text: India plans 30 GW offshore wind by 2030, with projects like Gulf of Khambhat targeting 5 GW. The National Offshore Wind Energy Development Policy supports this expansion.
learn.stat1: Global offshore wind capacity exceeded 60 GW in 2023, with Europe leading.
learn.stat2: Offshore turbines can generate 10-15 MW each, 30% more than onshore.
learn.stat3: India's offshore potential is 10,000 MW, with 1.5 GW installed as of 2024.
learn.stat4: Offshore wind reduces land-use conflicts, ideal for urban coastal areas.

learn.title: V2G Technology: EVs Stabilising the Grid 🚗⚡
learn.intro: Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology allows electric vehicles to send stored energy back to the grid during peak demand. This innovation enhances grid stability and maximizes renewable energy utilization.
learn.c1_text: EVs with bidirectional chargers can discharge stored electricity to the grid. A 60 kWh EV battery can provide 2-3 kW continuously, equivalent to a small household appliance. This reduces strain during heatwaves or outages.
learn.c2_text: V2G enables demand response, where EVs automatically adjust charging/discharging based on grid needs. For instance, during a blackout, 10,000 V2G-enabled EVs could supply 10 MW of power instantly.
learn.c3_text: India's FAME II scheme promotes V2G adoption. A pilot in Delhi showed 50 EVs could stabilize a 10 MW grid segment. With 10 million EVs by 2030, India could unlock 50 GW of V2G capacity.
learn.stat1: Global V2G market is projected to reach $10 billion by 2030.
learn.stat2: A single V2G fleet of 1,000 EVs can provide 5-10 MW of grid support.
learn.stat3: India aims for 30% EV sales by 2030, creating vast V2G potential.
learn.stat4: V2G can reduce grid peak demand by 15-20% in urban areas.

learn.title: Capacity Factor: Why Output Varies ⚙️
learn.intro: Capacity factor measures how much electricity a power plant actually generates compared to its maximum potential. It reveals why renewable sources like solar and wind have variable output despite high rated power.
learn.c1_text: Capacity factor = (Actual Output / Rated Output) × 100. A 100 MW solar plant with 20% capacity factor produces 18.4 MW on average. This metric helps compare efficiency across technologies.
learn.c2_text: Wind turbines depend on wind speed; solar panels on sunlight. For example, a 2 MW wind turbine in India might have a 30% capacity factor due to seasonal winds, generating 550 MWh monthly.
learn.c3_text: High capacity factors (40-50%) in wind farms reduce the need for backup power. In India, Rajasthan's wind farms achieve 35% capacity factors, supplying 8% of the state's electricity.
learn.stat1: Global average wind capacity factor is 35%, while solar is 15-25%.
learn.stat2: India's solar capacity factor ranges from 12-20% due to monsoon variability.
learn.stat3: A 1 GW wind plant with 40% capacity factor equals 8.76 TWh/year, equivalent to 2.4 million tons of coal avoided.
learn.stat4: Capacity factor impacts financial returns; lower factors require larger installations to meet demand.

learn.title: Small Wind Turbines for Homes 🏠🌀
learn.intro: Small wind turbines (up to 100 kW) are ideal for residential or community use. They provide decentralized power, reduce transmission losses, and empower remote areas with clean energy.
learn.c1_text: A 10 kW turbine can power a small home or farm. In India, a 5 kW turbine in Rajasthan's deserts meets 70% of a household's needs, costing ~₹2 lakh with 20-year lifespan.
learn.c2_text: Clusters of small turbines can serve villages. Gujarat's 10 MW community wind farm powers 5,000 homes, reducing diesel generator use by 90% and cutting CO2 by 25,000 tons annually.
learn.c3_text: India's goal is 500 MW small wind by 2030. Projects in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra target off-grid areas, aligning with the National Solar Mission's decentralized approach.
learn.stat1: India has 1,200 MW small wind capacity, with 10 MW installed in 2024.
learn.stat2: A 20 kW turbine costs ~₹3-4 lakh, cheaper than diesel generators.
learn.stat3: Small turbines can reduce rural electricity costs by 40-60%.
learn.stat4: Over 10,000 small wind systems are operational in India, mainly in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.
